title: E-Values Evaluating the Values of AI: Sheila Gulati and Nischal Nadhamuni
talk_summary: A VC and the CTO of Clarity (document-workflow automation) discuss why evals for generative/agentic systems are harder than classical ML evals and describe Clarity's pragmatic eval practices. Most of the talk is framing and values discussion, but the CTO's section has several concrete, copyable eval-process techniques.

takeaways.what_they_do: They deliberately do not build high-quality evals at the start of feature development; they frontload user testing to kill features that fail at the UX stage, then build evals once a feature is committed to production.
takeaways.evidence_quote: frontload the ux risk backload building out evals ... a lot of features die at the ux stage itself let them die before you build out evals

takeaways.what_they_do: They walk down a stack from end-user outcome to business value to adoption indicator to feature-health metric (e.g. JSON-answer variability), rather than measuring whatever is easy like F1.
takeaways.evidence_quote: think backward wordss from the user experience not forwards from what is easy to measure

takeaways.technique: Reduce degrees of freedom in model choice
takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of grid-searching LLM x prompt x customer combinations (thousands of prompts), they fix one LLM for the automated-prompt-engineering task and continuously re-evaluate as new models appear, accepting a small accuracy loss.
takeaways.evidence_quote: let's just use one llm for AP tasks not permanently and we'll continuously reevaluate as new llms come out

takeaways.what_they_do: They built their own synthetic data generation stack (after surveying 6+ vendors) and dedicate a team to monitor that synthetic data stays distributionally similar to real customer data, plus sanity-check accuracy on synthetic vs real.
takeaways.evidence_quote: part of their job is just monitoring that the synthetic data is distributionally similar to what we're seeing from customers

takeaways.what_they_do: They keep a lightweight wish-list eval for capabilities they may grow into (e.g. a quick mental-model test within an hour of a new model release) rather than requiring full benchmark-level metrics for unrequested workflows.
takeaways.evidence_quote: when gptv came out in about an hour we were able to say all right this is our mental model of how it's going to do
takeaways.numbers: ~1 hour to produce a first-pass eval

takeaways.technique: Don't treat silence as positive feedback
takeaways.what_they_do: They explicitly refuse to infer success from absence of user complaints and put the rigor burden on internal metrics, using user feedback only to close the loop.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we think it's very dangerous to assume that the absence of user feedback is positive feedback
